## 1. Plot temperature against failure. Fit a logistic regression model to this dataset and overlay the fitted model on the scatterplot.

```{r echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, error = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
#libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(boot)

#set a seed
set.seed(400)

#load in csv
oring <- read_csv("https://www.openintro.org/data/csv/orings.csv")

#create the failure variable
orig <- oring %>% 
  mutate(failure = case_when(
    #failure = 1 when there is a failure
    damaged > 0 ~ 1,
    # = 0 when there is no failure
    damaged < 1 ~ 0
  ))

#fit linear regression model
tempmod <- glm(failure ~ temperature, data = orig, family = binomial)

#graph the model (no confidence intervals)
ggplot(data = orig, aes(x = temperature, y = failure)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + 
  geom_smooth(
    method = "glm",
    method.args = list(family = "binomial"),
    se = FALSE 
  ) +
  labs(title = "Scatterplot of O-Ring Failure Versus Temperature", x = "Temperature", y = "Failure", caption = "*line indicates fitted logistic regression model for failure given temperature") +
  theme_bw()
```

## 2. The Challenger explosion occurred at 31 degrees. What is the predicted probability of an O-ring failure using your model? Note: This is an extrapolation is beyond the range of our data.

Our logistic model is as follows: logit(p of failure) = 15.0429 - 0.2322(temperature). So to find the predicted probability of the failure given the temperature is 31 degrees we get logit(p of failure) = 7.6125. So to get the probability of failure we can take $e^{7.6125} = 2023.3301$ and get a predicted probability of 2023.3301.

## 5. Create a histogram of the standard errors. Comment on its shape, spread and center. Compare the values to the standard error obtained by taking the standard deviation of the Beta1's. 

![Beta1 SE Parametric Histogram](/Users/naomiliftman/Desktop/MSDS/Data 557/simproj3/SEhist.png)
As we can see from our histogram, the SE for our parametric bootstrapped Beta1's is shaped the opposite of our Beta1s. While it is still heavily skewed this graph is skewed right. It is still unimodal, but our mode is at around 0.10, and the graph has a range from 0 to 1. 

When we get the SD for our Beta1's we get a value of 0.2201597. This is quite a bit higher than our mode SE for our Beta1's individually.

When we created a 90% confidence interval for each Beta1 which we collected we found that 9,772 of our 10,000 confidence intervals contained the true value of Beta1 (-0.2322).

## 11. Write a short paragraph constrasting and commenting on your findings from Questions 3-10.

What we found was that in the end the parametric bootstrap was far more accurate than the non-parametric when creating 90% confidence intervals. This makes sense. We know that a parametric bootstrap assumes that the data follows a specific distribution and if the data does indeed follow that distribution then the parametric bootstrap is very effective. And we know the data follows the binomial distribution because we are fitting logistic models, and their random component is indeed the binomial. 



# Apendix 
## 1. 
```{r message = FALSE, error = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
#libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

#load in csv
oring <- read_csv("https://www.openintro.org/data/csv/orings.csv")

#create the failure variable
orig <- oring %>% 
  mutate(failure = case_when(
    #failure = 1 when there is a failure
    damaged > 0 ~ 1,
    # = 0 when there is no failure
    damaged < 1 ~ 0
  ))

#fit linear regression model
tempmod <- glm(failure ~ temperature, data = orig, family = binomial)

#graph the model (no confidence intervals)
ggplot(data = orig, aes(x = temperature, y = failure)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + 
  geom_smooth(
    method = "glm",
    method.args = list(family = "binomial"),
    se = FALSE 
  ) +
  labs(title = "Scatterplot of O-Ring Failure Versus Temperature", x = "Temperature", y = "Failure", caption = "*line indicates fitted logistic regression model for failure given temperature") +
  theme_bw()
```

## 2. 
```{r}
summary(tempmod)
15.0429 - (0.2322*(32))
```

## 3. 
```{r}
B <- 10000
se_beta1 <- c(1:B)
boot_beta1 <- c(1:B)
conf <- data.frame(lower = NA, upper = NA)
count = 0
for(i in 1:B){
  predict_p <- predict.glm(tempmod, data = orig, type = "response")
  new_y <- rbinom(n = 23, size = 1, prob = predict_p)
  orig$new_y = new_y
  tryCatch({new_mod <- glm(new_y~temperature, data = orig, family = binomial)},
         warning = function(msg){
           count <<- count + 1 
         }
  )
  se_beta1[i] <- summary(new_mod)$coefficients[2, 2]
  boot_beta1[i] <- coef(new_mod)[2]
}
```

## 4. 
```{r}
bootsdata <- data.frame(boot_beta1, se_beta1)
ggplot(data = bootsdata) +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = boot_beta1)) +
  labs(title = "Histogram of Beta1's from the Parametric Bootstraps", x = "Beta 1", y = "Count") +
  theme_bw()
```

## 5. 
```{r}
bootsdata <- data.frame(boot_beta1, se_beta1)
ggplot(data = bootsdata) +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = se_beta1)) +
  labs(title = "Histogram of SE's from the Parametric Bootstraps", x = "SE for Beta 1", y = "Count") +
  theme_bw()
```

## 6. 
```{r}
#there are 22 df so t is 1.717
for(i in 1:B){
  conf[i,1] <- boot_beta1[i] - 2.074*se_beta1[i]
  conf[i,2] <- boot_beta1[i] + 2.074*se_beta1[i]
}
#true value is -0.2322
value = -0.2322
for(i in 1:B){
  conf$is_between[i] <- (value >= conf$lower[i]) & (value <= conf$upper[i])
}
#count
conf %>% 
  group_by(is_between) %>% 
  count(is_between)
```

## 7.
```{r}
B <- 10000
se_beta1_non <- c(1:B)
boot_beta1_non <- c(1:B)
conf_non <- data.frame(lower = NA, upper = NA)
count = 0
orig_2 <- orig %>% 
  select(temperature, failure)
for(i in 1:B){
  temp_resample <- sample(orig_2$failure, replace = T)
  full <- cbind(temp_resample, orig_2)
  tryCatch({new_mod_non <- glm(temp_resample~temperature, data = orig_2, family = binomial)},
         warning = function(msg){
           count <<- count + 1 
         }
  )
  se_beta1_non[i] <- summary(new_mod_non)$coefficients[2, 2]
  boot_beta1_non[i] <- coef(new_mod_non)[2]
}
```
